conclusion.justification: The report concludes that regular vitamin C supplementation does not prevent colds in the general population, explicitly supporting a 'no' answer based on systematic reviews.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
## Conclusion

For most people, the evidence supports "no" — regular vitamin C supplementation does **not** prevent colds in the general population. It can modestly shorten cold duration and severity once you catch one, and it may meaningfully reduce cold *incidence* only in a narrow subgroup (people under brief, extreme physical stress, like marathon runners).

## The Evidence

The most authoritative source is the Cochrane systematic review (Hemilä & Chalker), which pooled 29 trial comparisons involving 11,306 participants on regular vitamin C use (≥0.2 g/day) and found essentially no reduction in cold incidence in the general population (pooled risk ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.94–1.00) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/). The authors explicitly concluded that "the failure of vitamin C supplementation to reduce the incidence of colds in the general population indicates that routine vitamin C supplementation is not justified" (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/).

Notably, this same review found an exception: in five smaller trials (598 participants) involving marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers under subarctic conditions, regular vitamin C halved cold incidence — suggesting a benefit only under extreme physical/environmental stress, not for ordinary people (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/).

While vitamin C doesn't prevent colds for typical people, it does have a modest treatment effect once illness starts: Cochrane data show about a 9–10% shortening of cold duration with regular supplementation, and a 2023 meta-analysis found roughly a 15% reduction in symptom severity (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38082300/).

**Bottom line:** Your "no" is well-supported for cold *prevention* in typical adults, though vitamin C offers a small benefit for cold duration/severity and a larger preventive effect specifically for people under intense physical exertion.
